public_rationale: Marcus said that in November 2023 hallucinations were still rampant and LLMs still made many ridiculous errors. OpenAI's own GPT-4 page (March 2023) said GPT-4 has similar limits as earlier models and still hallucinates facts and makes reasoning errors. Vectara's November 2023 leaderboard found every tested model added unsupported facts when summarizing short documents, one at over 27%. In 2023 a law firm also filed fake court cases that ChatGPT had made up. Against this, OpenAI reported that GPT-4 hallucinated much less than earlier models, and GPT-4 scored about 3% on Vectara's test. So 'not a lot has changed' overstates things somewhat. But he hedged it with 'in some core sense', and his main point, that hallucination and basic errors remained a widespread unsolved problem, holds for the period.
limitations: 'Rampant' and 'ridiculous errors' are vague; the result depends on a plain reading.
No direct same-benchmark comparison between March 2022 and November 2023.
The legal-citation example comes from a news report, not the court record, which could not be read.

Target period is the GPT-4 era up to the post date, 2023-03-14 to 2023-11-16.

criteria.support_condition: Sources from the period show that leading LLMs, including GPT-4, still hallucinated facts and made reasoning errors often enough to be a recognized, unsolved problem, with documented real-world failures.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Sources from the period show hallucinations had become rare or largely solved in leading LLMs, or that basic errors were no longer common.

evidence.excerpt: Despite its capabilities, GPT‑4 has similar limitations as earlier GPT models. Most importantly, it still is not fully reliable (it “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors).
evidence.explanation: The developer of the leading model said GPT-4 has the same limits as earlier models and still hallucinates facts and makes reasoning errors. This supports the claim that the problem persisted.

evidence.excerpt: At the other end of the table, two Google LLMs fared much worse. A hallucination rate of over 27% for Google Palm-Chat suggests that its factual summaries of reference material are judged unreliable at best.
evidence.explanation: Vectara's November 2023 leaderboard found every tested LLM added unsupported facts even on a simple summarization task, with one major model above 27%. This supports the claim that hallucinations were still common across models.

evidence.excerpt: law firm Levidow, Levidow & Oberman got in trouble after they “submitted non-existent judicial opinions with fake quotes and citations created by the artificial intelligence tool ChatGPT.”
evidence.explanation: A widely reported 2023 case where ChatGPT invented court decisions. It fits the claim of serious, embarrassing errors. The report is dated November 2023; the court case itself happened earlier in 2023.

evidence.excerpt: While still a real issue, GPT‑4 significantly reduces hallucinations relative to previous models (which have themselves been improving with each iteration).
evidence.explanation: OpenAI reported measurable reductions in hallucination, which cuts against 'not a lot has changed'. It also calls hallucination 'still a real issue', which fits the core claim.
